summary: Provides terminology and methodology for benchmarking next-generation network security devices, such as next-generation firewalls and intrusion prevention systems. It covers test configuration parameters and testing approaches.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of rules for fairly testing how fast security guard devices on a network can work.

questions: how to benchmark a next-generation firewall
what is a device under test
what is the sustain phase in a benchmark
subtitle: How to test the speed of next-generation firewalls and intrusion prevention systems so results can be compared fairly.

tldr.problem: Firewalls grew from simple access-list filters into devices that inspect encrypted traffic and block exploits, and the old test method from 2003 no longer fit them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes the test setup, device features, client and server settings and traffic phases, then defines nine benchmarking tests plus a security-effectiveness check with KPIs such as throughput, connections per second and latency.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3511 and is informational: it is a lab method, not a protocol, meant to make vendor results reproducible and comparable.

today: RFC 9411 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 3511, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It is a testing method and not a protocol standard.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
It had been 18 years since the IETF first recommended test methodology for firewalls in RFC 3511. Since then, security devices added intrusion detection and prevention, threat management and analysis of encrypted traffic. RFC 9411 replaces that document and obsoletes it. RFC 2647 was consulted often and keeps its value.

The scope is next-generation firewalls (NGFWs) and intrusion prevention systems (NGIPSs) running in active, inline mode. The method first validates security effectiveness, then runs performance benchmarks. It is not meant for devices that rely on machine learning or behavioral analysis; if present, those features should be disabled. IP fragmentation tests from RFC 3511 were dropped because fragmentation no longer commonly occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: Old firewalls just checked a list of allowed visitors. New ones look inside every package, so they need a new way of being tested.

sections.title: The Test Setup
sections.content:
Everything happens in an isolated test environment. The Device Under Test / System Under Test (DUT/SUT) sits between test equipment that emulates clients and servers. Testers should avoid extra switches and routers, because the testbed must not become the bottleneck; Option 1 in the RFC, direct connection to the DUT/SUT, is the recommended layout.

The DUT/SUT must use one configuration for every test, in inline mode with fail-open disabled and logging enabled. Recommended NGFW features include TLS inspection, IDS/IPS, anti-spyware, anti-virus, anti-botnet, anti-evasion and application identification. If a recommended feature is off, the report must say why. A set of block and allow access-list rules scales with device size class: for example 5, 10, 20 or 50 application-layer block rules for XS, S, M and L.

The vulnerability set for security checks should reflect at least 500 CVEs from no older than 10 years, with a CVSS severity of High (7-10).
sections.plainLanguage: The test room is sealed off. A machine pretends to be thousands of visitors and websites, the guard box sits in the middle, and it must be set up the same way every time.

sections.title: Emulated Clients, Servers and Load Phases
sections.content:
Because results are strongly affected by transport settings, the RFC recommends concrete values. For TCP: a maximum segment size of 1460 bytes for IPv4 and 1440 for IPv6, an initial window of 65535 bytes, and up to three retries. For QUIC: 1232 byte UDP payloads for IPv6 and 1252 for IPv4, with 0-RTT and early data disabled.

Emulated browsers negotiate HTTP 1.1 or higher; for HTTPS they use TLS 1.2 or higher and must do a full handshake every time, with session resumption disabled to measure a worst case. Clients may use IPv4 and IPv6 in ratios from 100% IPv4 to 100% IPv6.

Each test runs through five phases: init, ramp up, sustain, ramp down and collection. Only the sustain phase is measured. The RFC recommends at least 5 seconds of init and at least 300 seconds of sustain, with a sampling interval under 2 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Every test has a warm-up, a steady run where the stopwatch is on, and a cool-down. Only the steady run counts.

sections.title: The Nine Benchmarking Tests
sections.content:
Section 7 defines nine tests: throughput with an application traffic mix; TCP connections per second with HTTP; HTTP throughput; HTTP transaction latency; concurrent TCP connection capacity with HTTP; and the HTTPS versions of the last four, which can also cover QUIC. Section 7 defines no QUIC-specific tests, but its HTTPS methodology can be used for QUIC and HTTP/3.

Each test uses three steps. Step 1 runs at an initial rate of 10% of the target to qualify the setup. Step 2 runs at the target. Step 3 iterates to find the maximum achievable value within the validation criteria. A typical criterion is that failed transactions and unexpected TCP resets stay under 0.001%, or 1 in 100,000. The connections-per-second tests recommend response object sizes of 1, 2, 4, 16 and 64 KB.

Latency tests measure Time to First Byte and Time to Last Byte. The single-transaction scenario closes the connection after one transaction; the multi-transaction scenario closes after 10.
sections.plainLanguage: The nine tests ask different questions: how fast can it pass data, how many new visitors per second, how many at once, and how long each waits. Each test starts gently and then pushes harder.

sections.title: Reporting and KPIs
sections.content:
Reports must give the date, hardware and software details of the DUT/SUT and the test equipment, enabled features, key parameters such as cipher suites and the IPv4/IPv6 split, and a prominent summary. Each test's KPIs must be documented separately, ideally with graphs over the sustain phase.

The defined KPIs are concurrent TCP and QUIC connections, TCP and QUIC connections per second, application transactions per second, TLS handshake rate, inspected throughput, Time to First Byte and Time to Last Byte. Throughput should be given in Gbit/s rounded to two places, and a transaction counts as successful for HTTP only with a valid status code of 200 OK.
sections.plainLanguage: After the race, everyone must hand in a full report card with the car, the track and every lap time, so others can check the result.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The tests belong in a laboratory-isolated environment. Testing with working exploits and malware carries risks, so access controls must keep them away from vulnerable networks. The recommended cipher suites are for test purposes only, and the optimal setting for performance may not be the most secure one.

IANA is asked for nothing. The RFC points to the existing benchmarking blocks 198.18.0.0/15 for IPv4 and 2001:2::/48 for IPv6; if more addresses are needed, it recommends private IPv4 ranges or IPv6 Unique Local Addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the test uses real attacks, it must be done in a locked room so nothing can escape into the real world.

viz.caption: THE FIVE PHASES OF A TEST RUN, IN ORDER

items.title: 1. Init
items.text: Layer 2-3 connectivity is set up; no measurements. At least 5 seconds recommended.

items.title: 2. Ramp up
items.text: Traffic grows from zero to the target objective; no measurements.

items.title: 3. Sustain
items.text: Constant load; all KPIs measured. At least 300 seconds recommended.

items.title: 4. Ramp down
items.text: Traffic slows to zero; no measurements.

items.title: 5. Collection
items.text: Test equipment merges and collates the report data.
